title: How to Get on Shark Tank: The Application Guide
meta_description: How to apply to Shark Tank: the two official routes, what open calls are actually like, what casting looks for, and how to spot the fee scams.
keywords: how to get on shark tank
how to pitch on shark tank

content.introduction:
There are exactly two official ways onto Shark Tank, and both of them are free. You either submit an application online through ABC's casting page, or you show up in person at an open call and pitch a casting producer for about a minute. That is the whole front door. Everything else you may have read about paid application packages, entry fees, and invite-only pitch weekends is either a different competition entirely or someone taking your money.

That matters more than it sounds, because the show's popularity has produced an entire industry of lookalike programs and outright scams that borrow its name. ABC is direct about this: all official communication from the Shark Tank casting team comes from email addresses ending in @sharktanktv.com. Anything from another domain is not from them.

This guide covers the two real routes, what the open calls are actually like on the day, what the casting team is looking for, and what happens in the long stretch between applying and standing on the carpet.

sections.heading: The Two Official Routes
sections.content:
Apply online. ABC runs an application form at abc.com/shows/shark-tank/apply. It opens when the show is actively casting for an upcoming season and closes when producers have what they need — for recent seasons the window has run through the spring. The first step is short: contact details, your occupation, a description of your product or business, photos, what stage you are at, and whether you are applying with co-founders. Many applicants are also asked for a brief video, typically a minute or two, introducing themselves and the business.

Attend an open call. ABC announces in-person casting events each season, held in a handful of cities. These are open to the general public — no invitation, no pre-screening. You complete a short application form, downloadable as a PDF from the casting page, and bring it with you filled in legibly, then wait your turn to pitch.

Neither route costs anything. There is no application fee, no processing fee, and no package you need to buy.

Open call schedules are announced per season rather than running continuously, so check the official casting page for what is currently open before making travel plans.

sections.heading: What an Open Call Is Actually Like
sections.content:
Expect a long day. Wristbands are handed out during a set window in the morning, and there is no advantage to arriving before it — the wristband, not your place in line, determines when you are seen. From there it is waiting, sometimes into the evening.

When your turn comes, you get roughly one minute to pitch a member of the casting team. The sharks are not there. Nobody at an open call is going to invest in you that day; the people you meet are producers deciding whether your business and your presence on camera are worth advancing to the next stage.

Practical details that trip people up: venues do not validate parking, bags may be searched at the entrance, and the events run in ordinary public spaces with neighbours, so the production asks attendees to keep noise and litter down.

One minute is less time than it sounds. It is enough for what you sell, who buys it, what you have sold so far, and why you are the person to build it — and not much else. Rehearse to that length rather than planning to compress on the spot.

sections.heading: What the Casting Team Looks For
sections.content:
Casting is choosing television as much as it is choosing businesses, and the two criteria pull in different directions.

On the business side, they want something real. A working product rather than a concept, and evidence that people are paying for it — revenue, retail placement, repeat customers, a waiting list. Early-stage is fine; hypothetical is not. They also want a business a shark could plausibly help, which usually means a consumer product with room to scale rather than a niche service.

On the television side, they want someone who can hold a scene. That means explaining your business clearly under pressure, having a reason you built it that an audience will remember, and being able to take a hard question without either crumbling or getting defensive. Charisma helps, but clarity helps more.

The single most common failure is not knowing your own numbers. Margins, cost of acquisition, lifetime sales, exactly how you arrived at your valuation — these come up in casting interviews long before they come up in the Tank, and vagueness there ends applications.

sections.heading: Eligibility
sections.content:
The application packet sets out the standard requirements for a US network reality programme: applicants must be at least 18, and US citizens or legal residents. People with felony convictions or pending criminal charges are excluded, as are employees of the show, its production companies and the network, and companies owned by the sharks — along with their immediate families.

If you are applying as a team, everyone who will appear on camera goes through the same process. Co-founders are not passengers on one person's application.

Requirements are restated in full in the paperwork you receive if you advance, and that paperwork is the authority — not this page, and not any third-party summary of it.

sections.heading: What Happens After You Apply
sections.content:
The short application is a filter, not the application. If producers are interested, they contact you and ask you to complete a much longer packet — a detailed document covering your business, your finances, your background, and the legal terms of appearing.

From there it is interviews, often by video, then background and legal checks on you and the business. Filming happens in Los Angeles in blocks over the summer, and selected entrepreneurs are flown out for their taping. A pitch that airs as eight minutes is typically filmed over an hour or more, and being filmed is not a guarantee of airing — some pitches never make it into an episode.

The whole process, from first application to broadcast, routinely runs close to a year. Persistence is a real factor: a number of entrepreneurs who eventually appeared were turned down on earlier attempts, and reapplying in a later season with more traction is a normal path rather than a fallback.

sections.heading: Scams and Lookalikes
sections.content:
Because casting is free and competitive, the gap gets filled by people charging for access. Some patterns to recognise:

Anyone charging an application fee. ABC's routes are free. A fee to apply, to be reviewed, or to be submitted to producers is not part of the process.

Emails from the wrong domain. Official casting correspondence comes from addresses ending in @sharktanktv.com. Treat anything else as unverified, however convincing the branding.

Paid pitch events using the show's name. There are legitimate startup competitions with entry fees, cash prizes, and investor panels — but they are separate events, not a route onto Shark Tank, even when their marketing implies otherwise.

Guaranteed placement. Nobody can guarantee you a spot, and anyone who says they can is selling something else.

If you are unsure whether something is genuine, go back to abc.com and follow the casting links from there rather than from a search result or an email.
